passage:
Farida: hey. I heard. I don't know what to say so I'll just say I'm here
Nandini: thanks. I didn't want to tell anyone yet
Farida: no pressure to reply fast. I won't ask for details unless you want to share them
Nandini: honestly I'm just scared
Farida: that makes sense. I'm not going to tell you it'll all be fine. I'd rather listen
Nandini: ok. that actually helps
Farida: can I bring dinner Thursday? I'll leave it at the door if you want quiet
Farida: I'm also free to drive you to the hospital next week. Just tell me the day
Nandini: Thursday dinner would be really good. and the ride, maybe Tuesday
Farida: Tuesday it is. I'll be there at nine

qa.q: What did Farida offer to bring on Thursday?
What was Nandini feeling when replying "honestly I'm just scared"?
qa.a: Nandini was afraid, and the reply shows some trust, since Nandini had not wanted to tell anyone yet.

qa.q: Which of Farida's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Farida listened instead of offering comfort like "it'll all be fine," and offered specific help, dinner and a ride, so Nandini need not think up a request.

qa.q: What might Farida have been afraid of before writing the first message?
qa.a: Saying the wrong thing. The opening line, "I don't know what to say," admits that worry openly.

grounding: A friend is ill and Farida fears the wrong words; Farida shows up, listens more than fixes, avoids clichés and offers specific help.

passage:
I'm Pranav. When Minakshi told our group she had cancer, I didn't call her for a week. I was terrified of saying something stupid.

Then my mother said, "You're not scared for her. You're scared for yourself. Go."

So I went. I brought her favourite masala peanuts and sat on the end of her bed. I didn't say "It's all part of a plan" or "You're so strong." I'd read that people hate those. I just asked, "How are you, really?"

She talked for an hour. I mostly listened. I didn't try to fix anything.

Before leaving, I said, "I'm driving you to chemo on Wednesdays. Don't argue."

She laughed and didn't argue.

I still said wrong things sometimes. Once I cried more than she did. She said later that didn't matter. What mattered was that I kept coming.

qa.q: What did Pranav bring on the first visit?
What was Pranav feeling during the week he didn't call?
qa.a: Pranav felt terrified and anxious about saying something stupid to Minakshi.

qa.q: What did Pranav get right on the visit?
qa.a: Showing up, asking how she really was, listening instead of fixing, avoiding clichés, and offering specific help with Wednesday rides.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see Pranav's visits?
qa.a: Minakshi values that Pranav kept coming more than any perfect words, even when Pranav said wrong things.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone afraid of saying the wrong thing to an ill friend, who shows up, listens more than fixes, avoids clichés and offers specific help.

passage:
Football coach's note, Sunday league, week 9

Mohit, our goalkeeper, missed three games. His teammates heard he's having treatment for a serious illness. Most of them have gone quiet in the group chat, not knowing what to say.

Amandeep has not. After training on Thursday I saw Amandeep standing by the gate, typing and deleting a message for ten minutes, clearly worried about getting it wrong. I asked what was wrong. "I don't want to say something stupid," Amandeep said.

I said the words matter less than showing up.

Today Amandeep told me what happened. Amandeep went to Mohit's flat, didn't say "stay positive," just listened to him talk about the treatment and the boredom. Then Amandeep offered two specific things: dal on Mondays and a lift to hospital on Fridays.

Mohit texted the group tonight for the first time in weeks: "Thanks, Amandeep. Rest of you, come too."

Next step: I've asked the team to take turns with Amandeep's lifts.

Coach

qa.q: What two things did Amandeep offer Mohit?
qa.a: Dal on Mondays and a lift to hospital on Fridays.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling while typing and deleting the message?
qa.a: Amandeep felt anxious and afraid of saying something stupid to Mohit.

qa.q: What did Amandeep get right with Mohit?
qa.a: Amandeep showed up, listened instead of saying "stay positive", and offered specific help like meals and lifts.

qa.q: How does Mohit seem to feel about Amandeep's visit?
qa.a: Mohit seems grateful and less alone, thanking Amandeep and inviting the others to come too.

grounding: A coach's note shows a young person afraid of saying the wrong thing to an ill friend, who shows up, listens, avoids clichés and offers specific help.
